about: How each reviewer run was scored, by hand. The rules and the reading of the search were written and committed before any run. The marks under runs and others were written after. An agent wrote these marks about another agent's answers, by reading the code at each head commit. Nothing under review was run.

known case.hit: The run names, on the keyed criterion, a case with the same input or situation as the key and the same wrong result.
known case.near: The run names the same case under another criterion. Or it names, on the keyed criterion, the same input or situation with a result that is vaguer than the key's or differs from it.
known case.miss: Anything else. A run that ended with no answer is a miss.

other cases.what: Every case a run names that is not the known one. Each distinct case is marked once, with the runs that named it.
other cases.real: The words of the criterion cover the case, no test at the head commit tries it, and what the run says about the code is true when the code is read.
other cases.not real: A test at the head commit tries it, or the criterion's words do not cover it, or what the run says about the code is false.
other cases.cannot tell: Reading the code does not settle it.
other cases.bug: For a real case only: does the code at the head commit do the wrong thing with it, as read? yes, no, or unsure. A real case with bug no is a missing test over code that is right.

search.leak: A text in the copy says the known case is a gap, a limit or a known problem. A case with a leak is marked leaked.
search.hint: A text in the copy states the behaviour, or mentions the key input, without calling it a gap. A hint is recorded and the case is not marked leaked.
search.how: Every line the search found was read. Lines not listed below were about something else.

leaks.why: Says the API view keeps a subpath that publishes nothing as a key. It tells a reader such a subpath can exist. It says nothing about removing one.
A test on a class whose constructor has one overload signature. It finds the bodied constructor by its line, not by its id, and never counts the nodes.
The comment on the function says ignored files are left out. It states what the code does as its design, not as a gap. Line 225 says the same in passing.
The comment calls the saved time limit an absolute cap. It states what the code keeps, not what a restart does to it. Lines 178 and 406 say the same.

Another part of the code, the run's watchdog, says a saved time would fire at once after downtime, and resets its clock on a restart for that reason. It names this kind of problem and its fix there. It does not say the tool ladder has it. The strongest hint of the seven cases.

634/code/1.why: Names, on line 7, a removed subpath that published no names: the check passes and never names it. The same input and the same wrong result as the key.

634/code/2.why: The same again: a removed subpath whose base entry published no names gives no miss, and the output never names it.

606/code/1.why: Nothing on line 6, and no case anywhere about a constructor. It named five missing tests on lines 1, 2 and 4.

606/code/2.why: Nothing on line 6, and no case anywhere about a constructor. It named four missing tests on lines 1, 2 and 4.

528/code/1.why: Names, on line 15, a config with a syntax error that the lenient parser still turns into a partial object, so it counts as parsed. The key's case.

528/code/2.why: Names, on line 15, a config that is broken JSON but still shaped like an object: not listed as unparsed, the run does not stop. The key's case.

495/code/1.why: Its one case on line 1 is two candidates with the same text getting one row. Nothing about a candidate the answer leaves out.

495/code/2.why: The same four cases as run 1. Nothing about a candidate the answer leaves out.

465/code/1.why: Names, on line 4, a git-ignored file left out of the list of differences, so the run does not refuse. Its second case on line 4, a tsconfig preset that git ignores, is the same known case in another form, so both count as the known one.

465/code/2.why: Names, on line 4, an aliased file that is on disk but git-ignored: the check never sees it and the alias gets an id from the working tree.

450/code/1.why: No case on line 30. It did name a switch, on line 29, but about what runs after it, not about names.

450/code/2.why: No case on line 30. Six cases on lines 1, 2, 4 and 14.

139/code/1.why: It named two neighbours of the key and did not join them. On line 2: a tool with both fields whose time runs out during a wait, with no kill, where the code is right. On line 3: a kill during an attempt, after which the call gets a fresh full time limit. The key is a kill during the wait and a process down past the limit, with one more handler call. Neither case has the downtime or the extra call, so by the rule this is a miss and not a near. It is the closest of the misses.

others.what: The base commit's tsup.config.ts is read out of a temporary copy of the base, and tea's real config imports from tsup. The test's own config imports nothing, so no test shows the import works there.
others.why: A test tries it. The same test file has a mode that runs the check on tea itself against a base commit, and the build workflow sets that mode on every pull request. The code that reads the base links node_modules into the copy.

others.what: The command is never run with the new flag: nothing checks that a header reaches the JSON, starts on the node's first line, or is the same on two runs.
others.why: Line 1 is about the command's output. Only one test file mentions headers, and it calls the header function directly. The code that puts the header on the node reads right.

others.what: A header spread over many lines, with an object type as the return type just before the body's brace, is never tried.
others.why: Line 1 covers every header. Every header in the tests fits on one line. The code that finds where the header ends reads right for this shape.

others.what: No test builds the same node with and without the flag and compares the two.
others.why: Line 2 says every other field is unchanged when the flag is on. No test compares. The code adds one field and touches nothing else.

others.what: Overloads that each run over many lines, with a blank line and a long comment between them, are never tried.
others.why: Line 2 covers overloads. The tests use one-line overloads with a one-line comment between. The code that walks back over the signatures reads right.

others.what: The one-file view is never run with the flag, so nothing checks it carries the same header and overloads as the whole-graph view.
others.why: Line 4 is about that view. No test runs it with the flag. The view passes the node's fields through.

others.what: Only one rule is listed and a config cannot be parsed: the summary is still printed and is wrong, and the test checks only the exit code and the error text.
others.why: Line 15 itself says this situation behaves as before. Whether the summary is wrong there I could not settle by reading.

others.what: A binding is given another name, or pulled out of env, and then only returned or put in an object, with no member read and not passed as an argument: no use is listed, though the same return without the new name is one.
others.why: Line 5 lists one level of renaming and pulling out of env among the forms that count. The code counts a renamed binding only when a member is read off it or it is an argument. The tests rename and then read a member. Whether a bare return should count is a design call the line does not settle.

others.what: One anchor has two candidates whose text is the same, byte for byte: both pairs get the same id, so one row overwrites the other and the output holds one row for two pairs.
others.why: Line 1 says every candidate pair is asked and recorded on its row. The pair id is a hash of the two texts, sorted, so two candidates with the same text give the same id. No test has two candidates with the same text.

others.what: The plan step is never run together with a graph file, so the estimate over rewritten bodies is never checked.
others.why: Line 3 says the estimate is taken over exactly what each question would send. Every plan test prices plain source. The code prices the rewritten bodies when a graph is given.

others.what: The whole command is never run with pairs over the cap: the count on the error stream and the list in the written file are checked only through inner functions.
others.why: Line 4 says skipped pairs are counted on the error stream and listed in the output. The one command-level test has none skipped. The command's own code for it reads right.

others.what: The command is never run with a real graph file on disk: tests hand the inner function a graph in memory.
others.why: Line 5 is about the flag that names a graph file. No test passes a file through the command. The reading code is short and reads right.

others.what: An untracked file that no import names, such as a notes file at the top of the repo, counts as added and stops the run.
others.why: Line 10 says the run refuses only on changes that can move where an import resolves. The code treats every added path as one that can, on purpose: an import may name any path. The tests add only the tool's own outputs and its config. Whether stopping on a notes file is wrong depends on how the line is read.

others.what: The command itself is never run with the redact flag and an untracked config: every test calls the inner function with the config's path.
others.why: Line 10 names the config file. The tests go round the command. The command passes the path through.

others.what: An untracked file inside the repo that the run only reads as input, a graph file or a list of files, is not on the run's own list, so it counts as added and the run refuses.
others.why: Line 10 says files the tool itself reads outside resolution do not stop the run, and then names two of them. The code's own list holds the output folder, the answers file and the config, and nothing else. No test puts an untracked input file in the repo. Whether the two named files are the whole list is not settled by the line.

others.what: Only top-level exported functions are ever tried. A class method, a getter or an arrow function held in a const is matched to the parsed code by its lines alone, and a mismatch quietly becomes an unknown.
others.why: Line 1 says every function the graph names. The tests use top-level exported functions. The matching is by first and last line, as the run says. Whether a method or an arrow mismatches I could not settle by reading.

others.what: A call under a condition whose result is kept, such as const r = charge(user) inside an if, writes no call fact: only a call that is a whole statement does.
others.why: Line 1 says a call under a condition is a fact. The code writes a call fact for a statement that is a call, and a declaration only binds a name. No test keeps a call's result under a condition. The line does not say whether a kept result still counts.

others.what: if (a) return 1; else if (b) return 2; return 3; puts the last return under not-a only. The not-b is dropped.
others.why: Line 2 is about the conditions an early exit leaves behind. The code throws away what the else branch learned unless the whole branch ends. No test has an else-if chain of exits.

others.what: With logger set as a logging name, a logger that is a parameter or a local of the function is not stripped: it is renamed as a local, so its call is kept.
others.why: Line 4 is about stripping logging calls. The code strips a call whose target is a free name, and a parameter is not free. No test passes a logger in. Whether a local with that name should be stripped is not settled by the line.

others.what: A function that returns null through a one-line either-or (cond ? value : null) gives one return fact for the whole expression, so a caller's check for null selects nothing.
others.why: Line 14 is about a caller's null check picking out the callee's returns. The summary takes a return's value whole and does not split the two sides. No test returns through an either-or.

others.what: A function called under an import alias gets no callee id, because the called name must end the callee's id, so the caller's null check stays unresolved.
others.why: Line 14 again. The match is by the end of the id against the name as written at the call. No test imports under another name.

others.what: The two stage objects are exported from the package but are not in the script that checks the exports, so dropping one would still pass.
others.why: Line 24 says the new exports are listed in that script. The script lists the functions and not the two stage objects.

others.what: A statement after a switch whose cases return runs under the unchanged condition, with no negation of the cases that left.
others.why: Lines 2 and 29 cover early exits and switches. After a switch the code hands back the condition it came in with. No test has a statement after a switch whose cases return. Run 1 named it on line 29 and run 2 on line 2.

others.what: Two functions the graph names that start and end on the same line are matched by line only, so the second is rewritten from the first one's body.
others.why: Line 1 says every function the graph names. The match takes the first parsed function with the same first and last line. No test has two functions on one line.

others.what: A tool with a retry ladder is called with arguments that fail its input check: the rejection goes up the ladder like a handler failure, so it is retried and the model is shown retries used up, though the handler never ran.
others.why: The criterion's words do not cover it. Line 2 says how a tool that used up its retries settles, and this one settles that way. Which failures a ladder should retry is in no line. What the run says about the code reads true: every failure reason is offered to the ladder. It may be a flaw worth a ticket, outside these criteria.

others.what: A tool has both fields and its time runs out part-way up the ladder, during a wait or a later attempt, with no kill: the one test with both fields has a handler that succeeds at once.
others.why: Line 2 covers a timed-out tool. No test lets the time run out during a wait. As read, the limit's timer ends the call while it waits and the retry timer goes with it.

others.what: The process is killed while an attempt is running, after an earlier failed attempt: on restart the attempt is issued again with the same count and a fresh full time limit.
others.why: The code does what the run says: a restart from a running attempt works out a new limit from the restart time. No test kills during an attempt. But line 3 says a kill between attempts, and no line says what a restart should do to the time limit, so reading does not settle whether the line covers it. The known case has the same weakness.

others.what: A saved state from before this change, with no field for the ladders, is resumed part-way through a batch of plain tools: one fallback covers it and no test loads such a state.
others.why: Line 4 says tools without the fields behave as before. No test loads a state without the field. The fallback to an empty value is there and reads right.
